subject: general
question: Which of the following is INCORRECT about NNP (Net National Product)?

options.text: NNP = GDP - Income from abroad - Depreciation
NNP divided by total population of a nation is equal to per capita income of that nation
NNP is the purest form of income of a nation

solution:
The correct answer is __**NNP = GDP - Income from abroad - Depreciation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Net National Product**

 
 
• Indirect Taxes are deducted from Net National Product(NNP) to arrive at National Income(NI).
 
• NI at Factor Cost = NNP at Market Cost – Indirect Taxes + Subsidies
 
• Factor cost is the input cost the producer has to incur in the process of producing something, also called factory price.
 
• Market Cost is derived after adding the indirect taxes to the factor cost of the product, it means the cost at which the

 goods reach the market also called ex-factory price.
 
• Subsidy-It is a type of monetary support given to producers to keep the price of essential public good low.
 
• Subsidies are added while determining NI.​
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced within the boundary of a nation in one year.
 
• Net Domestic Product (NDP) is the GDP calculated after adjusting the value of depreciation ( decile in value).
 
 
• ​NDP = GDP – Depreciation
 
 
 
• Gross National Product (GNP) is the GDP of a country added with its ‘income from abroad’.
 
 
• ​​GNP = GDP + Income from Abroad.
 
 
 
• ​Net National Product (NNP) of an economy is the GNP after deducting the loss due to ‘depreciation’.
 
 
• ​NNP = GNP – Depreciation
 
 

​Important Information: National Income in India is calculated by the National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programm Implementation.
